title: Hawks and doves: who wins?
hook: Hawks fight for the prize; doves share it. What mix does the population end up with?

knows: fitness comes from the meetings an animal has
doesNotKnow: that the population settles where hawks and doves score equally, a hawk share of V/C (here 2/3), from any start

misconception: Aggression always wins in evolution, so hawks take over.
objective: The learner can explain that hawks grow while rare (they take the prize from doves) and shrink while common (fights between hawks cost more than they win), so from 10% or 90% the hawk share settles at 2/3 = V/C, where hawks and doves score the same.

claims.text: With a prize of 4 and an injury cost of 6, the scores per meeting are: hawk vs hawk −1, hawk vs dove 4, dove vs hawk 0, dove vs dove 2.
claims.source: Hawk vs hawk: each wins half the time, (4 − 6)/2 = −1. Hawk vs dove: the hawk takes the prize, 4 and 0. Dove vs dove: they share, 4/2 = 2. Demo.tsx scoreH/scoreD. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: Derivation and Demo scoreH/scoreD: (4-6)/2 = -1, 4, 0, 4/2 = 2; matches the stage table.

claims.text: With hawk share x, a hawk averages 4 − 5x and a dove 2 − 2x; they are equal at x = 2/3, so hawks score more below 2/3 and less above it (at 10% hawks: 3.5 vs 1.8; at 90%: −0.5 vs 0.2).
claims.source: Hawk: −1·x + 4(1 − x) = 4 − 5x. Dove: 0·x + 2(1 − x) = 2 − 2x. Equal when 2 = 3x. Builder re-ran in Node, 2026-10-14. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: node hawk.mjs: H(.1) = 3.5, D(.1) = 1.8, H(.9) = -0.5, D(.9) = 0.2, equal at 2/3.

claims.text: In the stage's update rule (offspring = 10 + score, share x' = x·W_hawk / mean W), every start from 1% to 99% hawks reads 67% at generation 150, including the 10% and 90% starts.
claims.source: Builder's Node run, 2026-10-14 (deterministic, no random seed): all starts 1..99 round to 67% at generation 150; 10% gives 0.6666, 90% gives 0.6667; both 0.66667 at generation 400. The baseline 10 is a modelling choice that keeps offspring positive; it changes the speed, not where the share settles. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: node, Demo trajectory copied: all starts 1..99 round to 67% at generation 150 (10%: 0.66662, 90%: 0.66669). Baselines 5 and 20 settle at 2/3 too.

claims.text: When the cost of fighting exceeds the prize, the evolutionarily stable share of hawks is prize ÷ cost (here 4 ÷ 6 = 2/3).
claims.source: Maynard Smith J. (1982) Evolution and the Theory of Games, Cambridge University Press (hawk-dove game); Easley & Kleinberg (2010) Networks, Crowds, and Markets, ch. 7 (section unconfirmed). Attribution: fact-checker to confirm. The algebra is c2. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: Derivation: equal payoffs at x = V/C (c2), hawks gain below and lose above, so V/C is the stable mix. Maynard Smith 1982 not opened; secondary sources found by web search state ESS p = V/C for V < C. Easley and Kleinberg ch. 7 is 'Evolutionary game theory' (library catalogue via web search); the section (I believe 7.5, evolutionarily stable mixed strategies) is from memory and unconfirmed.

claims.text: The model is a toy: one-off meetings at random in a very large population, with chosen payoffs; it is not a claim about real animals.
claims.source: Model choice in Demo.tsx, stated in the reveal. · Fact-check pass 21 2026-10-14: VERIFIED: Demo model (deterministic shares, random pairing implicit, chosen payoffs) and the muted reveal paragraph say exactly this.

claims.text: When two hawks meet, each wins 4 or loses 6 with equal chance, so a hawk's average score against a hawk is (4 − 6) ÷ 2 = −1. (Stage line: 'Two hawks: win 4 or lose 6, so (4 − 6) ÷ 2 = −1.')
claims.source: Hawk-dove payoff (V − C)/2 with V = 4, C = 6, each hawk equally likely to win (Maynard Smith, Evolution and the Theory of Games, 1982, ch. 2; the payoff is the standard hawk-dove matrix, not opened in this session). Arithmetic: (4 − 6)/2 = −1. | Added 2026-10-14 (v2) by demo-builder.

recall.question: In the hawk-dove game, with fights costing more than the prize, why do hawks never take over the whole population?
options: When hawks are common they mostly fight each other and score less than doves
The share is set by the starting mix
recall.why: A hawk does best among doves. As hawks become common, costly hawk-vs-hawk fights drag their average below the dove's, so the share settles where the two score the same.
